p.src: The messenger crossed the river carrying the letter, but was seized by the troops guarding it and escorted before Sun Ce. Sun Ce read the letter and flew into a rage. He beheaded the messenger, then sent men to invite Xu Gong to discuss affairs under a show of goodwill. When Xu Gong arrived, Sun Ce showed him the letter and rebuked him: “Would you deliver me to my death?” He ordered his guards to strangle him. Xu Gong's family all fled and scattered. Three of his retainers wished to avenge Xu Gong, but bitterly lacked an opportunity.

p.src: One day Sun Ce led his troops on a hunt in the western hills of Dantu. They flushed out a great stag, and Sun Ce spurred his horse up the hill in pursuit. In the midst of the chase, he saw three men standing in the woods, carrying spears and bows. Sun Ce reined in his horse and asked, “Who are you?” They replied, “We are soldiers under Han Dang. We are hunting deer here.” Just as Sun Ce raised the reins to depart, one man thrust his spear at Sun Ce's left thigh. Greatly startled, Sun Ce hurriedly drew his sword and struck down from horseback, but its blade suddenly fell away, leaving only the hilt in his hand. Another man had already nocked an arrow and shot, striking Sun Ce squarely in the cheek. Sun Ce pulled the arrow from his face, took up his bow, and shot back at the archer, who fell as the bowstring sounded. The other two stabbed wildly at Sun Ce with their spears, shouting, “We are retainers of Xu Gong and have come expressly to avenge our master!” Sun Ce had no other weapon and could only fend them off with his bow as he retreated. The two fought to the death and would not withdraw. Sun Ce suffered several spear wounds, and his horse was wounded as well.

p.src: At this critical moment, Cheng Pu arrived with several men. Sun Ce cried out, “Kill the villains!” Cheng Pu and his men rushed forward together and hacked Xu Gong's retainers to mincemeat. When they looked at Sun Ce, blood covered his face and his wounds were grievous; so they cut strips from a robe with a knife, wrapped his wounds, and carried him back to Wuhui to recuperate. p.src: Now Sun Ce returned wounded and sent men to find Hua Tuo and ask him to administer treatment. Unexpectedly, Hua Tuo had already gone to the Central Plain; only a disciple remained in Wu, and he was ordered to treat Sun Ce. The disciple said, “The arrowhead was drugged, and the poison has entered the bone. You must rest quietly for a hundred days before you will be out of danger. If anger agitates you, the wound will be difficult to cure.”

p.src: Sun Ce was exceedingly impatient by nature and wished he could recover that very day. After resting for more than twenty days, he suddenly heard that a messenger from Zhang Hong had returned from Xuchang, and summoned him for questioning. The messenger said, “Cao Cao greatly fears my lord; and the advisers under his command all respect and admire you; only Guo Jia remains unconvinced.” Sun Ce asked, “What has Guo Jia said?” The messenger dared not answer. Sun Ce grew angry and pressed him relentlessly. The messenger had no choice but to report truthfully: “Guo Jia once told Cao Cao, ‘My lord is nothing to fear. He is rash and unguarded, impatient and poor in strategy—his is merely the courage of a common fighter. One day he will surely die at the hands of some petty man.’” Hearing this, Sun Ce flew into a rage and cried, “How dare that fellow presume to judge me! I swear I shall take Xuchang!” Without waiting for his wound to heal, he immediately sought to discuss sending out the army. Zhang Zhao remonstrated: “The physician warned my lord to remain at rest for a hundred days. Why, over a moment's anger, do you now make light of your body, worth ten thousand pieces of gold?”

p.src: While they were speaking, it was suddenly reported that Yuan Shao's envoy Chen Zhen had arrived. Sun Ce summoned him and questioned him. Chen Zhen explained fully that Yuan Shao wished to ally with Eastern Wu as an external support and attack Cao Cao together. Sun Ce was delighted. That very day he assembled his commanders in the tower over the city gate and held a banquet to entertain Chen Zhen. After they had been drinking for some time, he suddenly saw the commanders whispering among themselves and descending from the tower one after another. Puzzled, Sun Ce asked the reason. His attendants said, “A man known as the Immortal Yu is passing below the tower. The commanders merely wish to go and pay homage to him.”

p.src: Sun Ce rose and looked over the railing. He saw a Daoist in a crane-feather cloak, carrying a staff of goosefoot, standing in the middle of the road while all the people burned incense and prostrated themselves before him. Sun Ce angrily demanded, “What manner of sorcerer is that? Seize him and bring him here at once!” His attendants said, “His surname is Yu and his given name is Ji. He resides in the east and travels throughout Wu and Kuaiji. He freely dispenses charm-water and cures people of every illness; his remedies never fail. People today call him an immortal, so he must not be treated with disrespect.” Sun Ce grew still angrier and shouted the order, “Seize him immediately! Anyone who disobeys will be beheaded!”

p.src: His attendants had no choice but to descend and escort Yu Ji up the tower. Sun Ce rebuked him: “Mad Daoist, how dare you delude the people's hearts!” Yu Ji replied, “This humble Daoist is a priest of the Langya Temple. During Emperor Shun's reign, I once entered the mountains to gather medicinal herbs and found a divine book beside the spring at Quyang. Entitled The Way of the Great Peace and Azure Collar, it comprised more than a hundred scrolls, all containing methods for curing human illness. Having obtained it, I have sought only to proclaim Heaven's transforming teachings and bring relief to all people. I have never taken so much as a hair's worth from anyone; how can it be said that I delude the people's hearts?” Sun Ce said, “If you take nothing from anyone, where do your clothing, food, and drink come from? You are one of the same breed as Zhang Jue of the Yellow Turbans. Unless you are put to death now, you will surely become a source of future trouble!” He ordered his attendants to behead Yu Ji. Zhang Zhao remonstrated: “The Daoist Yu has been in Jiangdong for decades and has committed no offense. He must not be killed.” Sun Ce said, “For me to kill such a sorcerer is no different from slaughtering a pig or dog!” All the officials pleaded earnestly with him, and Chen Zhen also urged restraint. Sun Ce's anger had not subsided, but he ordered Yu Ji confined in prison for the time being. The officials all dispersed. Chen Zhen returned to his posthouse to rest.

p.src: Sun Ce returned to his residence, where an attendant had already related the affair to Sun Ce's mother, Dowager Lady Wu. The lady summoned Sun Ce to the inner hall and said, “I hear that you have placed the Immortal Yu in chains. He has often cured people's illnesses and is revered by soldiers and commoners alike. You must not harm him.” Sun Ce replied, “He is a sorcerer who uses black arts to delude the multitude. He must be eliminated!” The lady repeatedly tried to dissuade him. Sun Ce said, “Mother, do not listen to the wild talk of outsiders. Your son knows how to deal with him.” He then went out and ordered the jailers to bring Yu Ji before him for questioning. As it happened, the jailers all revered and believed in Yu Ji, and while he was in prison they had removed all his fetters; only when Sun Ce summoned him did they put the fetters back on and bring him out.

p.src: When Sun Ce learned the truth, he was furious. He punished the jailers severely, then had Yu Ji shackled and returned to prison. Zhang Zhao and several dozen others jointly signed a petition, bowed before Sun Ce, and begged to stand surety for the Immortal Yu. Sun Ce said, “You gentlemen are all learned men. How can you fail to understand reason? Once Zhang Jin, Inspector of Jiaozhou, put his faith in a perverse cult. He played zithers and burned incense, habitually wrapped his head in a red kerchief, and claimed this could increase his army's might—yet in the end enemy troops killed him. Such practices are utterly useless; you gentlemen simply have yet to perceive it. In seeking to kill Yu Ji, my true purpose is to forbid heresy and awaken the deluded.” Lü Fan said, “I have long known that the Daoist Yu can pray for wind and supplicate for rain. As the land is now stricken by drought, why not order him to pray for rain and thereby redeem his offense?” Sun Ce said, “Then I shall see what this sorcerer can do.” He accordingly ordered Yu Ji brought out of prison, had his fetters removed, and commanded him to ascend an altar and pray for rain.

p.src: Yu Ji obeyed the order. He bathed, changed his clothes, took a rope, and bound himself beneath the blazing sun. The watching townspeople packed the streets and blocked the lanes. Yu Ji said to the crowd, “I shall pray for three feet of blessed rain to save the people, yet in the end I shall not escape death.” The people said, “If your powers prove true, our lord will surely revere and submit to you.” Yu Ji said, “My allotted fate has reached its end; I fear there is no escape.”

p.src: Before long, Sun Ce came personally to the altar and gave the order: if no rain fell by noon, Yu Ji was to be burned alive. He first had a pile of dry firewood prepared and kept ready. As noon drew near, a violent wind suddenly arose. Where the wind passed, dark clouds gradually gathered on every side. Sun Ce said, “It is nearly noon. There are only dark clouds and no blessed rain—this proves he is a sorcerer!” He shouted for his attendants to carry Yu Ji onto the woodpile and set fire to it on all sides; the flames rose with the wind. Suddenly, a column of black smoke shot into the sky. With a tremendous crash, thunder and lightning burst forth together, and rain poured down in torrents. In moments, the marketplace became a river and every stream and ravine filled; a full three feet of blessed rain had fallen. Yu Ji lay face upward atop the woodpile and gave a great shout. The clouds dispersed, the rain stopped, and the sun appeared once more.

p.src: The officers and townspeople then helped Yu Ji down from the woodpile, untied his bonds, and bowed twice in gratitude. When Sun Ce saw officials and commoners alike prostrating themselves in the water without heed for their clothes, he flew into a rage and shouted, “Fair weather and rain follow the fixed ordinances of Heaven and Earth. This sorcerer merely chanced to take advantage of the moment. How dare you be so deluded and disorderly!” He drew his treasured sword and ordered his attendants to behead Yu Ji at once. The officers remonstrated with all their might. Sun Ce said angrily, “Do all of you mean to follow Yu Ji in rebellion?” The officers dared say no more. Sun Ce commanded a warrior to strike, and with one stroke Yu Ji’s head fell to the ground. At that moment, a stream of blue vapor was seen drifting away toward the northeast. Sun Ce ordered the corpse exposed in the marketplace as a warning, to punish the crime of sorcery and deception.

p.src: That night, wind and rain raged together. By dawn, Yu Ji’s corpse had vanished. The soldiers guarding the corpse reported the matter to Sun Ce. Sun Ce was furious and meant to execute the guards. Suddenly, a man came walking slowly from before the hall. When Sun Ce looked, it was none other than Yu Ji. Enraged, Sun Ce was just drawing his sword to cut him down when he suddenly fainted and fell to the ground. His attendants hastily carried him into his chamber and tended him; only after a long while did he regain consciousness. Lady Wu came to visit him in his illness and said, “My son, you wrongfully killed an immortal, and so have brought this calamity upon yourself.” Sun Ce laughed and said, “Since childhood I have followed Father on campaign and killed men beyond counting. When has that ever brought calamity upon me? Now that I have killed a sorcerer, I have removed a great evil. How could it instead become a calamity to me?” His mother said, “It is because you refused to believe that matters have come to this. You should now perform good works to avert the evil.” Sun Ce said, “My life is ordained by Heaven. A sorcerer can never bring calamity upon me. What need is there for rites of averting evil?” Seeing that she could not persuade him to believe, his mother secretly ordered her attendants to perform charitable deeds and rites to avert the calamity.

p.src: At the third watch that night, Sun Ce lay in his private chamber when a chill wind suddenly rose; the lamp went out and then flared alight again. In the lamplight, he saw Yu Ji standing before him. Sun Ce shouted, “All my life I have sworn to destroy sorcerous impostors and bring peace to the realm! Now that you are a ghost of the underworld, how dare you approach me!” He seized the sword at his bedside and hurled it, whereupon the apparition suddenly vanished. When Lady Wu heard of this, her anxiety deepened. Sun Ce therefore forced himself to walk despite his illness, hoping to ease his mother’s mind. His mother said to him, “The Sage said, ‘How abundant is the virtue of ghosts and spirits!’ He also said, ‘Prayers have been offered for you to the spirits above and below.’ One cannot refuse to believe in the affairs of ghosts and spirits. You wrongfully killed Master Yu; how could there be no retribution? I have already ordered a Daoist rite to be held at the Jade Purity Temple in the commandery. Go there yourself to worship and pray, and you will naturally recover.”

p.src: Sun Ce dared not disobey his mother’s command and had no choice but to ride reluctantly in a sedan chair to the Jade Purity Temple. The Daoists received him and asked him to burn incense. Sun Ce burned it but offered no obeisance. Suddenly, smoke rose from the incense burner without dispersing and formed an ornate canopy, atop which Yu Ji sat in solemn repose. Sun Ce angrily spat at him and cursed him. He ran out of the hall, only to see Yu Ji again, standing at its entrance and glaring fiercely at him. Sun Ce turned to his attendants and asked, “Do you see that demon ghost?” They all replied, “We see nothing.” Sun Ce grew still more furious, drew his sword, and hurled it at Yu Ji. A man was struck and fell. When the crowd looked, they saw it was the common soldier who had killed Yu Ji the day before. The sword had cut into his skull, and he died bleeding from all seven orifices. Sun Ce ordered the body carried away and buried.

p.src: By the time Sun Ce was leaving the temple, he again saw Yu Ji walking in through its gate. Sun Ce said, “This temple too is a lair that harbors demons!” He seated himself before the temple and ordered five hundred warriors to demolish it. Just as the warriors climbed onto the roof to strip away the tiles, they saw Yu Ji standing above them, hurling tiles to the ground. Sun Ce flew into a rage. He ordered all the Daoists expelled from the temple and had its halls set ablaze and destroyed. When the fire rose, Yu Ji appeared once more, standing amid the flames. Sun Ce returned angrily to his residence, only to find Yu Ji standing before its gate. Sun Ce therefore did not enter. Instead, he mustered the three armies, marched beyond the city, and made camp. He summoned his commanders to confer, intending to raise troops and aid Yuan Shao in attacking Cao Cao from two sides. The commanders all said, “My lord, your health is impaired; you must not move rashly. Wait until you have fully recovered. It will not be too late to send out the army then.”

u.src: By the time Sun Ce was leaving the temple, he again saw Yu Ji walking in through its gate.
Sun Ce said, “This temple too is a lair that harbors demons!”
He seated himself before the temple and ordered five hundred warriors to demolish it.
Just as the warriors climbed onto the roof to strip away the tiles, they saw Yu Ji standing above them, hurling tiles to the ground.
Sun Ce flew into a rage. He ordered all the Daoists expelled from the temple and had its halls set ablaze and destroyed.
When the fire rose, Yu Ji appeared once more, standing amid the flames.
Sun Ce returned angrily to his residence, only to find Yu Ji standing before its gate.

Sun Ce therefore did not enter. Instead, he mustered the three armies, marched beyond the city, and made camp. He summoned his commanders to confer, intending to raise troops and aid Yuan Shao in attacking Cao Cao from two sides.
The commanders all said, “My lord, your health is impaired; you must not move rashly.
Wait until you have fully recovered. It will not be too late to send out the army then.”

p.src: That night, Sun Ce slept in the camp and again saw Yu Ji approaching with his hair hanging loose. Within his tent, Sun Ce shouted and cursed without cease. The next day, Lady Wu issued an order summoning Sun Ce back to the residence. Sun Ce returned and went to see his mother. When she saw how haggard he looked, she wept and said, “My son, you have lost your former appearance!” Sun Ce at once took a mirror and looked at himself. Seeing how terribly thin and wasted he had become, he started in alarm and said to his attendants, “How have I grown so haggard?”

p.src: Before the words had left his mouth, Yu Ji suddenly appeared in the mirror. Sun Ce struck the mirror and gave a great cry. His wound burst open, and he fell senseless to the ground. His mother ordered that he be carried into his chamber. Presently he revived and sighed, “I shall not live again!” He then summoned Zhang Zhao and the others, together with his younger brother Sun Quan, to his bedside and charged them: “The realm is now in turmoil. With the people of Wu and Yue and the natural defenses of the Three Rivers, great deeds may yet be accomplished. Zibu and the rest of you, I trust you will assist my brother well.” He then took the seals of office and gave them to Sun Quan, saying, “If it is a matter of leading the hosts of Jiangdong, deciding strategy between two battle lines, and contending with the powers of the realm, you are not my equal. But in raising up the worthy, employing the able, and enabling each to exert his full strength in defense of Jiangdong, I am not your equal. Remember how hard your father and brother labored to found this enterprise, and plan wisely for yourself!”

p.src: Sun Quan wept bitterly, bowed, and received the seals of office. Sun Ce said to his mother, “My allotted years are spent, and I can no longer attend upon my beloved mother. I now entrust the seals of office to my brother. I beg you to instruct him morning and evening. Take care never to slight the old retainers who served Father and me.” His mother wept and said, “I fear your brother is too young to bear such great responsibilities. What are we to do?” Sun Ce replied, “My brother’s talents surpass mine tenfold; he is fully capable of bearing this great responsibility. If he cannot decide an internal matter, he may consult Zhang Zhao. If he cannot decide an external matter, he may consult Zhou Yu. I regret that Zhou Yu is not here, so I cannot charge him face to face!” He then called his younger brothers and charged them, “After my death, all of you must assist Zhongmou. If any member of the clan dares harbor disloyal intentions, you must join together and put him to death. Any kinsman who turns traitor must not be buried in the ancestral graveyard.” His brothers tearfully accepted his command. He then summoned his wife, Lady Qiao, and said, “It is our misfortune that you and I must part midway through life. You must care dutifully for my honored mother. When your younger sister comes to visit, whether morning or evening, ask her to convey my words to Master Zhou: he must devote himself to assisting my brother and not betray the deep friendship we have long shared.” When he had finished speaking, he closed his eyes and died. p.src: After Sun Ce died, Sun Quan collapsed weeping before his bed. Zhang Zhao said, “This is no time for you to weep, General. You should attend to the funeral rites while also managing the great affairs of the army and the state.” Sun Quan then checked his tears. Zhang Zhao ordered Sun Jing to oversee the funeral and asked Sun Quan to enter the hall and receive the civil and military officers who came to pay homage and offer their congratulations. Sun Quan had a square jaw and a broad mouth, blue-green eyes, and a purple beard. Formerly, when the Han envoy Liu Wan entered Wu and saw the Sun brothers, he told others, “I have closely observed all the brothers of the Sun family. Though each is gifted and distinguished, none is destined to enjoy his rank and fortune to the end. Only Zhongmou possesses an extraordinary and imposing appearance and a most uncommon frame. These are signs of the highest nobility; moreover, he will enjoy great longevity, beyond the reach of all the others.”

p.src: Now Sun Quan, in obedience to Sun Ce’s dying command, assumed charge of the affairs of Jiangdong. Before his administration was fully settled, a messenger reported that Zhou Yu was leading his troops back from Baqiu to Wu. Sun Quan said, “Now that Gongjin has returned, I have no cause for concern.” Zhou Yu had been defending Baqiu when he heard that Sun Ce had been wounded by an arrow, and so he returned to inquire after him; but as he approached Wu Commandery and learned that Sun Ce had died, he hastened there day and night to attend the funeral. Zhou Yu at once bowed and wept before Sun Ce’s coffin. Lady Wu came out and told Zhou Yu the words of Sun Ce’s dying charge. Zhou Yu bowed prostrate upon the ground and said, “How could I dare withhold the service of a dog or horse? I shall serve him faithfully until death!”

p.src: Presently, Sun Quan entered. When Zhou Yu had finished paying his respects, Sun Quan said, “I pray you do not forget my elder brother’s dying command.” Zhou Yu knocked his head upon the ground and said, “I would gladly spill my brains upon the earth to repay the kindness of one who understood me.” Sun Quan said, “Now that I have inherited the enterprise of my father and brother, by what strategy may I preserve it?” Zhou Yu replied, “From ancient times it has been said: ‘He who wins men prospers; he who loses them perishes.’ The present need is to seek a man of exceptional wisdom and far-reaching vision to assist you. Only then can Jiangdong be secured.” Sun Quan said, “My elder brother’s last words were that internal affairs should be entrusted to Zibu, while external affairs should depend entirely upon Gongjin.” Zhou Yu replied, “Zibu is a worthy and accomplished man, fully capable of bearing great responsibilities. But I lack ability and fear I may fail the weighty trust placed in me. I wish to recommend one man to assist you, General.”

p.src: Sun Quan asked who the man was. Zhou Yu replied, “His surname is Lu, his given name Su, and his style is Zijing. He is a native of Dongchuan in Linhuai. His breast contains the arts of war, and his mind conceals subtle strategies. He lost his father when young and has served his mother with the utmost filial devotion. His family is exceedingly wealthy, and he has often distributed his riches to relieve the poor and needy. When I was magistrate of Juchao, I passed through Linhuai with several hundred men. Being short of provisions, I heard that Lu Su’s household had two granaries, each containing three thousand hu of grain, and went to seek his aid. Lu Su immediately pointed to one granary and presented its entire contents to me. Such was his generosity. All his life he has delighted in swordsmanship, riding, and archery, and he has taken up residence in Qu’e. When his grandmother died, he returned to bury her in Dongcheng. His friend Liu Ziyang has invited him to go to Chaohu and join Zheng Bao, but Lu Su still hesitates and has not yet gone. My lord should summon him without delay.”

p.src: Sun Quan was overjoyed and immediately ordered Zhou Yu to go and engage him. Obeying the command, Zhou Yu went in person. After exchanging courtesies with Lu Su, he fully explained Sun Quan’s admiration for him. Lu Su said, “Liu Ziyang recently invited me to go to Chaohu, and I was about to accept.” Zhou Yu said, “Ma Yuan once told Emperor Guangwu: ‘In the present age, it is not only the lord who chooses his minister; the minister also chooses his lord.’ Our General Sun cherishes the worthy and treats scholars with courtesy; he welcomes men of uncommon talent and employs those of extraordinary gifts. Such a lord is rarely seen in this world. You need entertain no other plan. The proper course is simply to come with me and enter the service of Eastern Wu.” Lu Su followed his advice and accompanied Zhou Yu to meet Sun Quan. Sun Quan treated him with the greatest respect, and the two conversed all day without weariness.

p.src: One day, after all the officials had departed, Sun Quan kept Lu Su behind to drink with him. When evening came, they lay upon the same couch, feet touching. At midnight, Sun Quan said to Lu Su, “The House of Han now totters on the brink of ruin, and disorder reigns throughout the realm. I have inherited what remains of my father’s and brother’s enterprise and aspire to accomplish the deeds of Dukes Huan and Wen. What counsel would you offer me?” Lu Su replied, “In former times, Emperor Gaozu of Han wished to honor and serve Emperor Yi, but could not do so because Xiang Yu stood in his way. Cao Cao today may be compared to Xiang Yu. How then can you hope to become another Duke Huan or Duke Wen? In my humble judgment, the House of Han cannot be restored, nor can Cao Cao be swiftly eliminated. For you, General, there is only one plan: establish a third power in Jiangdong and watch for openings in the realm. While the north is burdened with many affairs, destroy Huang Zu, advance against Liu Biao, and occupy and defend all the lands along the Yangtze to its furthest reaches. Then proclaim yourself emperor and contend for the realm. Such was the enterprise of Emperor Gaozu.”

p.src: Sun Quan was overjoyed at these words, threw on his robe, rose, and offered his thanks. The next day he presented Lu Su with generous gifts and bestowed clothing, curtains, and other articles upon Lu Su’s mother. Lu Su in turn recommended another man to Sun Quan, a man of broad learning and many talents who served his mother with the utmost filial devotion. His double surname was Zhuge, his given name Jin, and his style Ziyu; he was a native of Nanyang in Langya. Sun Quan received him as an honored guest. Zhuge Jin advised Sun Quan not to establish relations with Yuan Shao, but to accommodate Cao Cao for the time being and then act against him when opportunity offered. Sun Quan followed his advice, sent Chen Zhen back, and gave him a letter severing relations with Yuan Shao.

p.src: Now Cao Cao, hearing that Sun Ce was dead, wished to raise an army and march south of the Yangtze. Zhang Hong, the Attendant Censor, remonstrated: “To attack a man during mourning is no righteous undertaking; and if we fail to conquer him, we shall cast aside friendship and create an enemy. It would be better to seize this occasion to treat him well.” Cao Cao approved his counsel and memorialized the throne to appoint Sun Quan a general, concurrently serving as Administrator of Kuaiji. He then appointed Zhang Hong Commandant of Kuaiji and sent him bearing the seal to Jiangdong. Sun Quan was delighted. Having also regained Zhang Hong in Wu, he immediately ordered him and Zhang Zhao to administer the government together. Zhang Hong also recommended a man to Sun Quan. The man’s surname was Gu, his given name Yong, and his style Yuantan; he had been a disciple of the Palace Gentleman Cai Yong. He was a man of few words who drank no wine, stern in manner and upright in character. Sun Quan appointed him chief assistant and made him acting Administrator. From that time onward, Sun Quan’s might resounded throughout Jiangdong, and he won the wholehearted support of the people.
